description: The skeleton of every web page: doctype, html, head, and body.

screens.body:
Every HTML page starts with <!DOCTYPE html>. It's a note to the browser that says "this page follows the modern HTML rules."

It's not a tag, so it has no closing partner and nothing inside it. Just one line, at the very top, every time.

Skip it and browsers fall back to "quirks mode" — old, unpredictable rendering you never want.

options: Tells the browser this is a modern HTML page
Displays a title at the top of the page
check.question: What does <!DOCTYPE html> do?

code.snippet:
<!-- display-only: the first line of every page -->
<!DOCTYPE html>

screens.heading: Your very first line: the doctype
screens.keyPoint: <!DOCTYPE html> goes first, always — it's a declaration, not a tag.

screens.body:
After the doctype, everything on the page lives inside one <html> ... </html> pair. It's the root — the box that holds all the other boxes.

Add lang="en" to it (or whatever language the page is in). Screen readers use it to pronounce words correctly, and search engines like it too.

One tiny attribute, real accessibility win.

options: So screen readers pronounce the text correctly
So the page gets a spell-checker
check.question: Why add lang="en" to the <html> tag?

code.snippet:
<!-- display-only: the root element -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <!-- everything goes here -->
</html>

screens.heading: The html wrapper
screens.keyPoint: <html> wraps the whole page; lang tells the browser the page's language.

screens.body:
Inside <html> there are exactly two big sections. The first is <head> — the backstage area. Nothing in here shows up on the page itself.

The head holds information ABOUT the page: its title, the character set, links to stylesheets, and little notes for search engines.

Think of it like the label on a file folder: you read the label, not the folder's contents.

code.snippet:
<!-- display-only: backstage info -->
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>My First Page</title>
</head>

screens.heading: The head: the page's backstage
screens.keyPoint: <head> holds info about the page — none of it is visible.

screens.body:
The one head element you'll notice daily: <title>. Its text shows in the browser tab, in bookmarks, and in search results.

"Untitled Document" tabs are a small crime. A good title says what the page is: "SwiftGigs — Find local gigs", not "Home".

It lives in the head, but its effect is very visible — it's the first thing people see before the page even loads.

options: In the browser tab and bookmarks
As a big heading at the top of the page
check.question: Where does the <title> text appear?

code.snippet:
<!-- display-only: naming the tab -->
<head>
  <title>SwiftGigs — Find local gigs</title>
</head>

screens.heading: The title tab
screens.keyPoint: <title> sets the browser tab text, bookmarks, and search result name.

screens.body:
The second big section is <body> — the stage. Every heading, paragraph, image, button, and form on the page goes in here.

If it's visible to a visitor, it's inside the body. If you accidentally put visible content in the head, browsers will quietly drag it into the body anyway — but don't rely on that.

Head = about the page. Body = the page.

check.question: A paragraph visitors should read goes inside…

code.snippet:
Hello!

This is what visitors see.

screens.heading: The body: what people actually see
screens.keyPoint: Everything visible goes in <body>. Head is backstage, body is the stage.

screens.body:
HTML elements wrap inside each other like nesting boxes: holds and , and holds headings, paragraphs, and more. Tags must close in reverse order — like stacking and unstacking.

Hello there

is correct;

Hello there

is tangled. Indent nested elements (two spaces is the norm). The browser doesn't care, but future-you reading the code absolutely does.
screens.heading: Nesting: boxes inside boxes
screens.keyPoint: Close tags in reverse order; indent so nesting is easy to see.

screens.body:
Sometimes you want to leave a note in the code that visitors never see: <!-- like this -->.

Comments are invisible on the rendered page. Use them to mark sections ("<!-- NAVBAR -->") or to explain a tricky bit of markup.

They're also handy for temporarily hiding a chunk of the page while you test — wrap it in a comment instead of deleting it.

options: Nothing — comments are invisible on the page
The comment text in small grey letters
check.question: What does a visitor see of <!-- a comment -->?

code.snippet: Welcome!

screens.heading: Comments: notes to yourself
screens.keyPoint: <!-- comments --> are invisible on the page — notes for humans only.
